    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

    According to recent reports, the platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or launched an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

    You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.

    We have a cohort of smaller video businesses where retention is not where it should be. Nobody owns it today. You will. The revenue that stays in that segment, and the revenue that grows inside it, is yours.

    It has been revealed that this is a coaching role for someone with a growth marketer's mindset. We wouldn't hire a demand gen marketer who couldn't analyze the state of the business and figure out what's needed, and we won't hire a coach who can't either. You'll look at a customer's business the way an owner would: where the revenue comes from, where it leaks, and what to do next. You pull your own numbers to get there. When a customer needs a custom report to answer a growth question, you build it yourself.

    In a recent development, it's a one-to-many job. Your cohort is larger than a 1:1 book, so the work is designing coaching that scales: cohort programs, group sessions, office hours, and triggered outreach when the data says a business is drifting. You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

    Recent findings suggest that success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

    Industry observers note that A coach with a growth marketer's mindset. Maybe you've run growth or demand gen for a small business, built your own audience, or coached founders through their numbers. You understand how a membership business makes money, you pull your own analytics to see what's working, and you're comfortable doing it in front of a client. What matters is that you can find the real constraint in a business, then sit with the operator and say the honest thing.

    Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each manufacturer’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft mentioned they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    In a recent development, anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI indicates it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an crucial step,” writing in a tweet that the tech giant supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    Partner Solutions Architect , AI Builder at Supabase

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • Supabase is the backend of choice for a growing wave of AI-native builders, and we're deepening structured partnerships with the platforms they build on top of — Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.
    • We’re looking for a Platform Solutions Architect to join our Success Team and help embed Supabase into the Solutions and Engineering communities with AI Builders.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Supabase is the backend of choice for a growing wave of AI-native builders, and we're deepening structured partnerships with the platforms they build on top of — Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable. These partners' teams are talking to thousands of developers and agents who need exactly what we build—a full backend platform with Postgres at the core—without the vendor lock-in. This is an opportunity to get Supabase in front of the right partner SAs and make us the default recommendation for a modern, AI-ready backend.

    We’re looking for a Platform Solutions Architect to join our Success Team and help embed Supabase into the Solutions and Engineering communities with AI Builders.

    Sources indicate that you’ll work closely with Partner Solutions Architects and Partner Engineers at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, helping us proactively identify builder problems where Supabase is the right solution and closing the gap between partner intent and real developer outcomes. This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions of AI-native apps and agents.

    In this role, you’ll focus on three core pillars:.

    Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

    Develop and deliver technical workshops, training materials, and enablement content to give partner SAs the fluency to position Supabase.

    Create demos, integration guides, and reference architectures that make Supabase’s fit with Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable immediately legible.

    Partner with SAs at these companies on active opportunities to move deals forward and feeding technical pipeline intelligence back to the alliance lead.

    Resolve blockers for partner SAs working on Supabase implementations to maintain their credibility with the builders they support.

    Troubleshoot complex integration scenarios and turn solutions into reusable assets.

    Maintain a close feedback loop with Supabase product and engineering teams to ensure technical guidance reflects the latest platform capabilities.

    Measure success through co-sell opportunities sourced, influenced deals, and SA enablement metrics across the Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable partnerships.

    Write technical blog posts and case studies that demonstrate real-world Supabase implementations built on Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.

    Represent Supabase at conferences, meetups, and partner-sponsored events (e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI dev days, Vercel Ship, Lovable community events).

    Develop video content and interactive learning experiences to reduce the "time-to-fluency" for partner SAs.

    Have 5+ years of experience in technical roles with deep hands-on experience building on modern AI infrastructure. Previous experience working at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Lovable (or a similar AI builder platform) or as a partner to one is required.

    Understand how partner SAs at AI builder platforms are incentivized, how they make recommendations, and how the partner ecosystem influences developer decisions.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences, explaining complex concepts with ease.

    Have a strong technical foundation in PostgreSQL, APIs, and modern development frameworks like React and Next.js, plus fluency with AI/agent tooling (LLM APIs, MCP, agent frameworks).

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving rapidly to build a playbook from scratch.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Industry observers note that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    #112674. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1213 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    Industry observers note that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    According to recent reports, “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres noted. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    It has been revealed that to reach upcoming audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    In a recent development, “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” stated Torres, who is right now a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Recent findings suggest that mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres stated. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Sources indicate that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    Industry observers note that “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres noted. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    Sources indicate that “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he noted. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    It has been revealed that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler remarked. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres remarked. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler noted.).

    “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Part of the problem, he mentioned, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    Recent findings suggest that but this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one organization or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Sources indicate that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    It has been revealed that collins claims The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently remarked no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Upcoming Orleans Bowl.

    I love Upcoming Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and remarked it straight up: "No.".

    We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Latest Orleans Bowl might be out, several at the moment-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a significant part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Newly introduced York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In a recent development, in another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar mentioned. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    According to recent reports, redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I stated there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics.     This isn’t another product job.

    It’s the chance to define a newly introduced category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.

    Science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

    A chance to build an AI-native Product Department.

    You’ll be working with the most complex data in the world : the human mind.

    Deep inside you are looking for a latest adventure with….

    🚀Ambition around AI field : Smart teammates driven to create an iconic, international product.

    🔥Impact : you strive to make a real difference in the organization's growth, and not be a number in a major organization.

    😍Mission : knowing your greatness left a mark in people's lives, through technology and behavioral science.

    At Paradox, we believe that greatness is trainable.

    That’s why we want to empower people at scale by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals),.

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    This is why we are looking for a PM to make Paradox a category-defining global brand loved for its product.

    This is a full-time position from our beautiful offices in Dubai, Paris or Lisbon or remotely anywhere in the world.

    We believe self-help is broken.Most learning platforms are used the same way : consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

    At Paradox, we believe people deserve more.More than content. More than motivation.

    They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    We believe that every human learns differently, and that technology can do more than entertain or save time.It can translate insight into transformation, through AI personalization, lean experimentation, and deep psychological understanding.

    Because learning shouldn’t just make you feel inspired for a day, it should change how you live, think, and create.

    At Paradox, we want to re-invent how people grow.

    We do not build another course or coaching app but the Operating System for Greatness.

    Founded by David Laroche - a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson, and Gad Elmaleh, Paradox aims to build something that will live beyond any individual (including its founder), for decades to come.

    Our ambition is to compete with players like Mindvalley (150M ARR), but with a sharper vision, grounded protocols for achievers, people who want more for their life, refusing mediocrity.

    To do that, we bring together designers, tech, coaches, and filmmakers to create learning experiences that are cinematic, precise, and effective.

    We move fast, aim high, and hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify, and MasterClass. No fluff, focused on meaningful impact.

    While others hide their numbers, we want to let our results speak loudly for us.

    Get obsessed with transforming our clients’ lives and let those transformations be our marketing.

    We want to build an AI-native company, with agents in every department doing the work alongside our people.

    In product, that means building a self-learning AI for product management: a system that learns from every user signal, experiment and release, and gets sharper at deciding what to build next.

    For our clients, it means a self-learning AI that serves them through psychology and coaching, and gets better at helping each person change with every interaction.

    You won’t just use AI tools: you’ll help design the agents, loops and feedback systems that make Paradox learn faster than anyone else.

    -----------------------------------------.

    As Product Manager, you’ll be the architect of a newly introduced category, transforming growth into a living ecosystem powered by AI, behavioral science, and design.

    You won’t just build features, you’ll craft experiences that rewire behavior.

    You’re the architect bringing clarity between vision and execution, the person who turns “we should build this” into “it’s live, here’s the data and tangible impact.”.

    Every product cycle you lead will integrate:.

    Protocols : guided frameworks grounded in psychology that rewire perception, emotion, and action.

    Pods : human connection, accountability, and shared rituals.

    Loops : adaptive, AI-powered coaching cycles that evolve with each user.

    Personalization : experiences that feel uniquely theirs, every time.

    Industry observers note that going from a successful personal brand, to an international tech-driven iconic brand, is far from easy. It will be messy, chaotic - requiring constant iterations on MVPs and innovation in tech. Therefore to achieve this here are :.

    -----------------------------------------.

    Translate the founder’s strategic vision into a clear product strategy.

    Build and maintain the roadmap that connects business goals, user outcomes, and technological innovation.

    Ensure every feature supports the evolution of the Paradox ecosystem: Loops, PX Agents, Protocols, Membership.

    Be obsessed with user problems : talk to people weekly, analyze patterns, and identify where transformation breaks.

    Turn insights from behavioral science, coaching psychology, and learning design into actionable product hypotheses.

    Design loops, feedback, and rituals that make growth tangible.

    build for both the heart (inspiration) and the brain (structure).

    Apply Lean Startup methodology and scientific thinking to validate ideas through MVPs, not opinions.

    Design experiments and measurable success metrics before building.

    Iterate on a weekly basis on new hypothesis.

    Define and track product success metrics (activation, retention, transformation rates).

    Connect data to business KPIs, know how your product drives lifetime value, not just engagement.

    We don’t track metrics just for internal dashboards, we track them also to prove transformation.

    Help marketing leverage this data to fuel authentic, evidence-based storytelling — showing the world what real transformation looks like.

    Create a visceral experience that translates into emotions of inspiration, awe from customers.

    Use a Science-backed, Cinematic, Contrarian style : Every product touchpoint should be grounded in behavioral science, expressed with cinematic beauty, and challenge conventions.

    -----------------------------------------.

    3–6 years as a Product Manager / Product Owner in EdTech, SaaS, or Consumer Tech.

    Bonus: experience in AI-driven products, learning design, or personal development platforms.

    You’ve shipped at least one major feature or product end-to-end, and can show measurable results.

    Uses Figma comfortably, prototypes directly.

    Craft-obsessed : You get things done, you love to work much beyond 9-5, you have a doer mentality, a bias for outcomes and want to be a beast in your field.

    User & Impact Obsessed: You think in outcomes, not outputs, you care about transformation.

    Analytical & System Thinker: You can turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, metrics, and roadmap.

    Digital & AI savvy : you’re able to build AI Agents (if not, you demonstrate ability to learn while applying).

    Cross-disciplinary Curiosity: You speak both tech and human; You can move from vision to spreadsheet to Figma.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the firm to scrape the websites of Meta Business account people.

    On Thursday, the firm took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an enhancement to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Sources indicate that meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not blueprint to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Recent findings suggest that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the manufacturer was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    Sources indicate that in the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    That’s why we want to empower people at scale by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals),.

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    This is why we are looking for a Head of product to make Paradox a category-defining global brand loved for its product.

    This is a full-time position from our beautiful offices in Dubai, Paris or Lisbon or remotely anywhere in the world.

    We believe self-help is broken.Most learning platforms are used the same way : consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

    According to recent reports, at Paradox, we believe people deserve more.More than content. More than motivation.

    They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    We believe that every human learns differently, and that technology can do more than entertain or save time.It can translate insight into transformation, through AI personalization, lean experimentation, and deep psychological understanding.

    Because learning shouldn’t just make you feel inspired for a day, it should change how you live, think, and create.

    At Paradox, we want to re-invent how people grow.

    We do not build another course or coaching app but the Operating System for Greatness.

    Founded by David Laroche - a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson, and Gad Elmaleh, Paradox aims to build something that will live beyond any individual (including its founder), for decades to come.

    Our ambition is to compete with players like Mindvalley (150M ARR), but with a sharper vision, grounded protocols for achievers, people who want more for their life, refusing mediocrity.

    To do that, we bring together designers, tech, coaches, and filmmakers to create learning experiences that are cinematic, precise, and effective.

    We move fast, aim high, and hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify, and MasterClass. No fluff, focused on meaningful impact.

    While others hide their numbers, we want to let our results speak loudly for us.

    Get obsessed with transforming our clients’ lives and let those transformations be our marketing.

    We want to build an AI-native manufacturer, with agents in every department doing the work alongside our people.

    In product, that means building a self-learning AI for product management: a system that learns from every user signal, experiment and release, and gets sharper at deciding what to build next.

    For our clients, it means a self-learning AI that serves them through psychology and coaching, and gets better at helping each person change with every interaction.

    You won’t just use AI tools: you’ll help design the agents, loops and feedback systems that make Paradox learn faster than anyone else.

    You won’t just build features, you’ll craft experiences that rewire behavior.

    You’re the architect bringing clarity between vision and execution, the person who turns “we should build this” into “it’s live, here’s the data and tangible impact.”.

    Every product cycle you lead will integrate:.

    Pods : human connection, accountability, and shared rituals.

    Loops : adaptive, AI-powered coaching cycles that evolve with each user.

    Personalization : experiences that feel uniquely theirs, every time.

    Build and maintain the roadmap that connects business goals, user outcomes, and technological innovation.

    Ensure every feature supports the evolution of the Paradox ecosystem: Loops, PX Agents, Protocols, Membership.

    Be obsessed with user problems : talk to users weekly, analyze patterns, and identify where transformation breaks.

    Turn insights from behavioral science, coaching psychology, and learning design into actionable product hypotheses.

    Design loops, feedback, and rituals that make growth tangible.

    build for both the heart (inspiration) and the brain (structure).

    Apply Lean Startup methodology and scientific thinking to validate ideas through MVPs, not opinions.

    Design experiments and measurable success metrics before building.

    Iterate on a weekly basis on latest hypothesis.

    Define and track product success metrics (activation, retention, transformation rates).

    Connect data to business KPIs, know how your product drives lifetime value, not just engagement.

    We don’t track metrics just for internal dashboards, we track them also to prove transformation.

    Help marketing leverage this data to fuel authentic, evidence-based storytelling — showing the world what real transformation looks like.

    Create a visceral experience that translates into emotions of inspiration, awe from owners.

    Bonus: experience in AI-driven products, learning design, or personal development platforms.

    You’ve shipped at least one major feature or product end-to-end, and can show measurable results.

    Uses Figma comfortably, prototypes directly.

    Craft-obsessed : You get things done, you love to work much beyond 9-5, you have a doer mentality, a bias for outcomes and want to be a beast in your field.

    User & Impact Obsessed: You think in outcomes, not outputs, you care about transformation.

    Analytical & System Thinker: You can turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, metrics, and roadmap.

    Digital & AI savvy : you’re able to build AI Agents (if not, you demonstrate ability to learn while applying).

    Cross-disciplinary Curiosity: You speak both tech and human; You can move from vision to spreadsheet to Figma.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    --------------------------------.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

    ✅ If you’re obsessed with systems, psychology, and design…✅ If you dream of using AI to amplify what makes us human….

    Build a product that fuses neuroscience, design, and AI to reinvent how humans grow.

    The chance to build a product that could redefine human potential.

    Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

    In the heart of our headquarters stands the 100 000 Dreams Wall,.

    Every photo on that wall is a life rewritten:.

    “I found peace with my father.”.

    -> Playing a crucial role in the development of a firm whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

    -> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

    -> ❤️ Contributing to the Paradox Foundation (our non-profit), dedicated to empower teenagers.

    But that's not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    -> 😎A tech giant culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    -> 🌎A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    -> 🏤Magnificent office in Dubai, Paris, Lisbon - it feels like home :).

    -> 🧍‍♀️Standing desks paid by the organization if you live far from our offices.

    -> 💻Work on Mac, for us it counts :).

    -> 🏀350€ per year paid by the company to take care of yourself ( for your gym, or dance class or whatever make you feel great).

    -> 📚150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

    -> 🔥6 1:1coachings - A Paradox Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

    If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀🚀🚀.

    That job description resonated with you?

    Here is your tailor made hiring process.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey (with a short video assignment).

    💻 A 30mn video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

    💻 A 1h video call with Timy, HR, to discuss how you'd fit into Paradox’s Product team.

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss Product Vision and the next milestones to build.

    💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

    According to recent reports, our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

    We also want you to have time to ask all of your questions regarding the mission, the long-term vision of your team and the firm, our values, with the relevant interlocutor in front of you.

    If you believe design and AI can awaken what’s best in us then this isn’t a career move.

    Latest Update: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    A fresh study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    Sources indicate that A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less crucial — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    According to recent reports, participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how crucial the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty upcoming. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how notable the work is.”.

That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    In a recent development, and aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write.

    Tech Report: Senior Product Builder - Hub at Camunda

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.
    • Camunda Hub is where enterprises run Camunda at scale.
    • Take over Hub's fleet propagation mechanism from the team building its first version, and make it work for access, secrets, tenants, licences and custom roles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Camunda Hub is where enterprises run Camunda at scale. From Hub they manage their clusters and tenants, decide who can do what, and roll changes out across the whole organization. We’re looking for a Senior Product Builder to own the backend and architecture that let Hub manage a whole fleet of clusters. Your first focus will be the mechanism that sends access, secret, tenant and licence changes out to every connected cluster and brings deployments, health and audit records back. From there, you’ll shape Hub’s foundations: its event model, the service boundaries and data model other teams build on, and how Hub behaves when things fail or get upgraded. The platform is your product. Your users are platform administrators, Centres of Excellence and the builders across Camunda who depend on what you create. You’ll join a fresh two-person pod in our remote-first team. You’ll have real ownership as the person who makes the call, and you’ll build AI-first, from written specs through to production. Our customers run mission-critical processes on Camunda, so your work will matter to them every day.

    Take over Hub's fleet propagation mechanism from the team building its first version, and make it work for access, secrets, tenants, licences and custom roles.

    Write short design documents for foundational changes, get them reviewed by the teams that depend on them, and turn them into tested, shipped code.

    Design how Hub behaves when things go wrong: offline clusters, partial failures, Hub outages, and clusters being adopted or detached.

    Build the path from clusters back to Hub, starting with deployment inventory, health, audit records and licence status.

    Design Hub's first event and webhook mechanism, so admins and agents can react to changes instead of polling for them.

    Join the pod's rotations and Hub on-call, and help other builders take on backend work through reviews, guidelines and contract tests.

    What You Will Bring to the Role:.

    Experience building and running backend systems in production that other teams or customers depend on.

    Comfort taking a problem nobody owns yet and turning it into a design, a proposal and shipped code.

    Product judgment for technical users: you talk to the people who use your APIs and make trade-offs on their behalf.

    Clear, short writing that lets a remote team review and decide asynchronously.

    Care for how a system behaves when parts of it fail, not only for the happy path.

    Designed and shipped a control plane or similar system that pushes desired state to many targets. Knows outbox or event-log patterns, idempotent apply, versioning, retries and drift reconciliation.

    Senior backend engineering in Java (API design, relational data models, multi-tenant SaaS services) and hands-on Helm and Kubernetes for self-managed installations.

    Software architecture and failure analysis: partial failure, blast radius, consistency trade-offs. Has debugged production incidents in a distributed system and is ready for on-call.

    Has shaped an API or platform as a product, and writes design docs other teams can build on. Gets agreement across teams without formal authority.

    Builds AI-first from written specifications and checks AI output as carefully as any other code.

    Kubernetes operators or GitOps tools, for example Argo CD.

    OIDC, SCIM and permission models, or secret managers and licence systems.

    Camunda 8 or another workflow or orchestration engine.

    Enough frontend skill to build a thin UI on top of a backend capability.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    #LI-AM1 #LI-Remote #C1 #USEAST #USWEST.

    We offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    The Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market. Final offers depend on skills, experience, and location, and we typically hire in the first half of the range to allow room for growth:.

    United States: $143,800.00 to $231,900.00.

    United Kingdom: £90,300.00 to £148,500.00.

    Singapore: S$178,600.00 to S$267,900.00.

    Canada: C$152,700.00 to C$251,200.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Blueprint (VSOP).

    It has been revealed that we invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.
